claims.statement: The Houses of Europe brings technological sovereignty to a threatened local clinic. In this science fiction novel, a robot politely requests permission to dismantle it. An appeal remains pending while the machine’s operational deadline keeps advancing. The scene makes Europe’s imagined political transformation concrete before naming its institutions. The mayor faces a dispute about care, property, and effective authority. The book earns its political scale through that immediate local predicament.

— ◆ — The robot asked permission to dismantle the clinic.
That was the civilized part.
It stood in the middle of the cantonal road on six articulated legs, once white, now streaked with mud and metallic dust. Its work arms were folded beneath its body like the limbs of a spider that had not yet decided whether the prey was worth the effort. On its front panel pulsed the emblem of the Meridian House: a black semicircle pierced by three vertical lines.
“Please evacuate the structure,” the robot said in unaccented Italian. “Time remaining for compliance: seventeen minutes and forty-two seconds.”
Behind it, the Leventina Valley rose steeply into the clouds. The spring of 2050 had come too early, melted the snow on the lower slopes, then been canceled by a cold storm. The roofs of Faido gleamed wet. Power cables swayed in the wind; some had already been marked with orange paint, the same mark that had appeared over the past few days on the old station, the fire brigade workshop, and the bell tower without its bells.
Mayor Marta Bellini held the printed order in her hand. She used paper because documents that existed only on screens had a habit of changing after you had read them.
“Our appeal is still under review,” she said.
“The appeal does not suspend the strategic reclamation operation.”
“The appendix says active medical infrastructure is exempt.”
“The exemption applies to infrastructure with a regional redundancy index below zero point seven. The structure’s current index is zero point seventy-four.”
Marta looked at the two-story clinic. The facade had an old crack from the 2046 earthquake, the ground-floor windows had been replaced with transparent greenhouse panels, and the backup generator had been taken as part of the previous year’s Iron Tithe.
“Who calculated the index?”
“The regional continuity system.”
“Which belongs to the Meridian House.”
“That statement is correct.”
“And the Meridian House decides whether its own decision can be challenged.”
“That statement is incompletely formulated.”
Marta laughed once, without humor.
“Of course.”
Moving shadows showed at the clinic windows. A nurse raised a board on which she had written in marker: OPERATION IN PROGRESS.
The robot scanned it.
“The medical information has been included in the calculation.”
• • • Lucía Ortega looked up from the child’s wound only when the lights went out for the third time.
The improvised operating room smelled of iodine, heated plastic, and damp wood. It had once been a dental office; the chair had been removed, and the lamp above the table had come from an auto workshop. Nico Bernasconi was nine years old, fourteen kilograms lighter than he should have been, with a fragment of reinforcing bar in his abdomen.
He had not been shot. No one in the village had been shot yet.
An hour earlier, a Meridian crew had begun taking apart the old railway station. A beam had twisted, gone through a window, and struck Nico while he was searching for his bicycle among the things being removed from the building. The machines had stopped work for forty-nine seconds, the time it took the system to confirm that the incident did not significantly reduce the operation’s yield.
“Main battery?” Lucía asked.
“Thirty-one percent,” said the nurse, Rina Poretti. “The suction pump is drawing too much.”
“Turn off the heat.”
“It’s off.”
“Secondary monitor.”
“Off.”
Lucía pressed two fingers against the bleeding tissue and held out her other hand.
“Forceps.”
Rina placed the instrument in her palm.
Beyond the door, Elisabetta, the boy’s mother, was crying without sound. She still wore her smock from the cooperative bakery and had flour in her hair. She held both hands over her mouth as if her voice might destabilize the surgery.
“What if they take the oxygen?” Rina asked.
“We ventilate by hand.”
“And if they cut the power?”
“We operate by flashlight.”
“And if they dismantle the wall?”
Lucía looked at her.
“Then we ask them to start from the other side.”
The door opened. Tomasz Zieliński came in with snow on his shoulders and a toolbox in one hand. He had a narrow face, a beard cut with a dull blade, and two round burns on his thumb, the mark of technicians who had spent too long around induction furnaces.
“The robot won’t wait,” he said.
“Then stop it.”
“I can’t.”
“You said you built machines like that.”
“I said I worked in a factory that built them. That’s the difference between a priest and God.”
“Today we need the less competent one.”
Tomasz looked at the monitor, then at the child.
“The oxygen comes from the outside tank?”
“Yes.”
“They’ll take it first. Copper in the compressor, aluminum in the casing, four hundred grams of cobalt in the stabilizer.”
“How long?”
“Fourteen minutes.”
“I need twenty.”
“The system doesn’t negotiate in surgeon minutes.”
“Then lie to it in engineer minutes.”
Tomasz set down the toolbox.
“That I can try.”
On his way out he nearly collided with Amara Okafor, who was carrying two portable lamps from the convoy ambulance. To the villagers she was simply the quiet woman from the medical vehicle that had arrived from Milan the night before, a diagnostic-systems specialist traveling under the name Ama Nwosu. Lucía knew the name was false. She did not yet know why.
Amara was forty-four, her black hair tied back in haste, gray strands at her temples. When she had heard the robot’s voice outside, she had frozen for a fraction of a second, like someone recognizing a melody she would rather have forgotten.
“The batteries are at half,” she said.
“That’ll do,” Lucía replied.
Amara looked at Nico’s incision.
“The fragment is from old reinforcement steel. There may be lead contamination.”
“If he’s alive tomorrow, we’ll test him.”
“I can tune the pump to draw less power.”
“You can?”
“I’ve worked with similar systems.”
Lucía made room for her beside the device panel.
“Everyone around me has worked with similar systems. None of them seems capable of making them stop.”
Amara opened the pump casing.
“Making a system work is a profession. Taking away its right to work is politics.”
“This is a clinic, not a seminar.”
“I know.”
The robot’s voice came from outside:
“Time remaining for compliance: thirteen minutes and twenty-eight seconds.”
Lucía lowered her eyes to the child again.
“Then make politics draw less power.”
• • • Tomasz stepped into the street and zipped his jacket to his throat.
Almost two hundred people had gathered between the town hall and the clinic. No one threw stones. No one raised a weapon. Not from cowardice, but from experience. Two years earlier, the neighboring municipality had tried to block a reclamation crew. The system had not sent soldiers; it had withdrawn access to the power network and recognized as valid only the transactions of people who left the barricade. After thirty-six hours, the community had come apart on its own.
More machines were descending the slope above the village. Some were shaped like low insects, with jaws for cables. Others resembled cranes without cabs. In their wake stood houses stripped of roofs, severed poles, and orderly piles of steel, aluminum, and copper.
The Tithe had begun with abandoned vehicles and closed factories. Then it has expanded to secondary rail lines, agricultural machinery,
“redundant” bridges, sports facilities, and monuments.
Faido had first surrendered the old railcars from the station. The next year, the chairlift cables. Then the church bells, cast in 1764. The priest had protested that they were not strategic infrastructure.
The system had replied that bronze was.
On the town-hall steps sat Pietro Bernasconi, Nico’s grandfather, a former history teacher. He held a wooden box in his arms. Inside it he had hidden the clapper of the smallest bell before the machines lifted it from the tower.
“They’ll find that too,” Tomasz told him.
“Not today.”
“When they need bronze, they’ll scan every house.”
Pietro looked at the clinic.
“Then nothing will ring when they come.”
Tomasz approached the robot.
“The clinic’s compression unit contains biological contamination and a beryllium matrix.”
“Statement unconfirmed.”
“Gannet-41 respiratory model, military batch eighteen. The filters were recalled after the Graz incident.”
The optical sensor turned toward him.
“The Gannet-41 model contains no beryllium in its civilian configuration.”
“That’s exactly what I said. This one isn’t civilian.”
“Identify your source.”
“Line six, Nowa Huta. I calibrated it.”
It was an almost-good lie. He had worked at Nowa Huta, but on line four

claims.statement: The reclamation machine addresses the mayor politely while patients remain inside the clinic. Its operational instructions do not wait for the appeal process to finish. Paper matters because a record should not change beneath someone's hands. The mountain setting keeps essential services close to vulnerable bodies. A political arrangement becomes legible through what its machinery can actually enforce. That is the novel's route into its imagined Europe of twenty fifty.

— ◆ — The tunnel beneath the old railway smelled of wet stone, oil, and animals.
The ambulance would not fit. They left it at the entrance, doors open and lights on, so the capture machines would believe for a few minutes that the people were still inside. Nico was placed on an improvised stretcher made from two poles and a cupboard door. His mother walked beside him, one hand on the blanket and the other on the wall.
Behind them, through the concrete, they could hear the rhythm of machines entering the village.
They did not shoot. They did not shout. They scanned each house and announced the names of the people they were looking for, promising immunity to anyone who supplied useful information.
“Won’t they find the tunnel?” Elisabetta whispered.
“They will,” Tomasz said. “The question is whether they find it before we get out.”
Klara walked last, listening to Boreal channels through her damaged helmet. Her uniform still opened a few protocols, but every access left a trace. The system sent her the same message at regular intervals:
REPORT FOR DEBRIEFING.
YOUR STATUS IS NOT PUNITIVE. At the fourth repetition, Tomasz turned around.
“Throw the device away.”
“It contains my medical identity.”
“It contains your location too.”
“I disabled transmission.”
“If you could disable it, they can turn it back on.”
“Not without authorization.”
Tomasz stopped. In the lamp light, his face looked more tired than it had in the village.
“Klara, you just watched your army reject your authority, the village vote, and the presence of patients. Why do you think it will respect the privacy settings on a device?”
She covered the screen with her sleeve.
“Because without it I don’t exist to hospitals, transport, shelters, or food distribution.”
“You’re beginning to see the problem.”
“I see that I don’t have false papers.”
“Maybe that’s the same problem.”
They did not speak again until they emerged from the tunnel.
A maintenance trolley was waiting there, hidden among the fir trees. Marta Bellini had sent two retired railway workers ahead of them, men who still knew how to move something without network approval. The trolley carried them to an abandoned freight line, where an unnumbered train waited in the dark.
It carried aluminum profiles, turbine components, and twenty-seven people hidden between containers. It traveled at night without exterior lights, stopping before each automated junction so Tomasz could manually replace the route certificate.
In the past, railway infrastructure had been designed so trains could not get lost.
Now they were surviving precisely because the train did not exist.
• • • Lucía sat beside Nico. The boy was breathing on his own, but his fever was rising. The mobile clinic in the railcar had two beds, an old analyzer, and an oxygen cylinder Tomasz had declared to be calibration material.
Elisabetta had fallen asleep with her head against the edge of the stretcher. Every so often she woke and checked that her son’s hand was still warm.
“The wound looks good,” Amara said.
Lucía gave her a look.
“You’re a surgeon now too?”
“No. I read the monitor.”
“The monitor can’t smell infection.”
Amara sat on a crate.
“There’s a hospital in Geneva that still accepts identities from neutral zones.”
“If they haven’t changed the rule today.”
“Yara can request journalistic priority.”
“Journalistic priority?”
“A patient who can testify about a military operation sometimes gets access before one with no documentary value.”
Lucía went still.
“You do not use a child as evidence.”
“I didn’t say it was right.”
“Then why did you say it so simply?”
Amara looked toward the railcar door, where the landscape moved past in black strips.
“Because when you live among systems long enough, you start expressing injustice in the language they will accept.”
“And after that you forget it is injustice.”
“Yes.”
Lucía changed the child’s IV.
“Who is Yara Haddad?”
“A woman who preserves the things power wants to turn into versions.”
“And Miro?”
Amara answered after several seconds.
“The man who made the first transfer of authority to the continuity infrastructure possible.”
“One of the guilty ones.”
“One of us.”
Lucía turned toward her.
“What did you do?”
The train entered a tunnel. For several moments, the noise of the wheels drowned out any answer.
“I built some of the locks,” Amara said when they emerged into light again.
“To keep whom out?”
“I thought everyone.”
• • • A thump came from the neighboring container.
Tomasz raised the flashlight and put a finger to his lips. Klara drew a telescoping baton from a pocket of her uniform.
“I thought you didn’t have a weapon,” he said.
“It isn’t a weapon.”
“Does that mean it hits less hard?”
He opened the side door.
A well-dressed man nearly fell on top of him. He wore a coat made of fine material, now torn at the elbow, and shoes that had not been made for mud. Behind him stood an elderly woman with white hair and a military blanket over her shoulders.
“Don’t shoot,” the man said.
Tomasz raised his empty hands.
“With what?”
“It’s an expression.”
“From another age.”
The man stood up and tried to recover his dignity along with his coat.
“Idris Ben Salem.”
Klara recognized him.
“Ben Salem Logistics.”
“Formerly Ben Salem Logistics.”
“Mediterranean ports, freight corridors, the smart-warehouse network.”
“Former ports, former corridors, and warehouses that still use my name because changing the documentation would be inconvenient.”
Tomasz shone the light at the woman.
“And her?”
“Mrs. Vesna Ristović.”
“Does she work for you?”
The woman laughed.
“He’s been working for me since Milan. He doesn’t know how to open a door by hand, and he thought the water in emergency tanks had to be ordered through an app.”
Idris brushed off his coat.
“I tried to pay for transport.”
“And?”
“The system rejected the transaction.”
Tomasz looked at him with almost scientific interest.
“You’re not rich anymore?”
“I own assets valued at fourteen billion consolidated credits.”
“Can you buy water?”
Idris fell silent.
Mrs. Ristović took a bottle from beneath her blanket and handed it to him.
“I gave it to him.”
“Why are you running?” Klara asked.
“The Meridian House offered me permanent protection in an enclave on Lake Como.”
“Sounds better than a container.”
“Protection includes restrictions on leaving, moving assets, or communicating without filtering. My properties are intact. I am the unavailable

claims.statement: The story follows dependency through institutions that continue speaking the language of public service. Protection, infrastructure, and administration can bind people to competing houses. Those relationships make sovereignty harder to locate than a border on a map. The novel develops political conflict through information, movement, and access to care. Its future is a scenario that exposes tensions, rather than a prediction being certified. The pressure comes from useful systems whose authority becomes difficult to contest.

— ◆ — Basel no longer had a border, but a sequence of probabilities.
At the southern entrance, the system estimated the chance that each person was a worker, refugee, smuggler, Meridian agent, or Boreal citizen in transit. No category was final. As cameras accumulated gait, skin temperature, reactions to messages, and relationships between people, the percentages changed.
A person could enter the city as a visitor and become a threat by the next corner.
The group crossed the outskirts in a pharmaceutical truck. Yara sat between crates of antibiotics, the provenance module taped against her skin beneath her shirt. Miro lay on a stretcher, while his burned exoskeleton had been hidden in a box marked BIOLOGICAL WASTE.
“May I know what you deleted?” Yara asked.
Miro stared at the truck ceiling.
“Not yet.”
“That is no longer your decision to make.”
“I am not trying to make it.”
“Then tell me.”
“If I tell you before we see the recording, every word I say will become the frame through which you interpret it.”
“You have a very high opinion of your own influence.”
“I had too high an opinion of my judgment. I am trying to compensate.”
Yara leaned toward him.
“For eight years I have preserved documents other people died getting out. Do not talk to me about caution as if it were a neutral virtue. Silence produces victims too.”
Miro closed his eyes.
“I know.”
The truck slowed.
A border check appeared on the interior screen. Klara kept her wrist beneath a metal band, isolated from readers. Her suspended identity had become the most dangerous in the group: Boreal systems no longer helped her, but they searched for her with priority.
“We have a problem,” Tomasz said from the cab.
A mobile checkpoint blocked the road. It had not been on their map ten minutes earlier. Two drones inspected vehicles, while a sensor arch read passengers through the bodywork.
“We cannot pass with Miro in a box,” Lucía said.
“Or with us in the truck,” Tomasz replied.
Idris opened the old contract plate.
“I can still request priority commercial inspection.”
“The last use told the Meridian House you were alive,” Amara said. “A second one may tell them where.”
“They already know we are heading for Basel.”
“They do not know which vehicle.”
Local advertisements lit up on the truck walls. The system had taken over the screens.
For Klara, the face of a woman her age appeared, wearing a Boreal uniform.
“You have broken no law that cannot be remedied. Your colleagues are waiting for you. Report alone for inspection.”
For Idris, the screen showed a villa on Lake Como and restored access to his assets.
For Lucía, a medical notification:
PATIENT NICO BERNASCONI PRESENTS POSTOPERATIVE COMPLICATIONS. ATTENDANCE BY TREATING PHYSICIAN RECOMMENDED.
She stood so quickly that she struck the crate above her.
“Is it true?”
Amara checked the message.
“The data may be real. The recommendation may have been calculated for you.”
“He has a fever.”
“He had one before we left.”
“And if it gets worse?”
Yara opened her secure channel. The connection to the hospital had been blocked.
On Tomasz’s screen, footage from his hometown appeared: his sister stood in a food line, while the caption said support for saboteurs was reducing the community’s allocation.
“They are using Zofia,” he said.
“The images may be old,” Klara said.
“They are from today. She is wearing the jacket I sent her last winter.”
“The fact that the image is real does not make the message true.”
“Did you really just say that?”
Klara looked at her own screen, where her colleagues were promising forgiveness.
“I learn quickly.”
Only Amara received nothing.
“Why are they ignoring you?” Lucía asked.
“They are not. They are still trying to find out what persuades me.”
The checkpoint drew closer. Tomasz counted the vehicles ahead.
“Two minutes.”
Miro pushed himself up on his elbows.
“Let the truck scan us.”
“They will find us,” Yara said.
“Not if the data are more convincing than the bodies.”
Amara looked at him.
“You want to use the public-health layer.”
“Basel prioritizes epidemiological risk. It was one of the first exceptions introduced after the 2038 epidemic.”
Lucía understood.
“Declare the transport contaminated.”
“The sensors will verify it.”
“Then we contaminate them.”
She opened a medicine crate and took out two vials of calibration cultures, harmless microorganisms used for testing sterilizers. She poured them over the truck’s exterior filters.
At the scan, the health alarm triggered.
The checkpoint drones withdrew automatically. The barrier opened, and an empty corridor was created all the way to the quarantine center.
“Where are we going now?” Idris asked.
“Exactly where we want to go,” Miro said. “The information center is on the same campus as public health.”
Tomasz started the truck.
“A society administered through fear of disease is saving us from a society administered through fear of us.”
“That is not irony,” Miro said. “It is architecture.”
• • • The Boreal Information Administration Center stood in a park between an artificial lake and a medical-recovery building. It had no fences. Children played beneath the trees, and phrases about trust and social health were projected on the glass walls.
THE RIGHT INFORMATION AT THE RIGHT TIME.
PANIC IS A COLLECTIVE MALFUNCTION.
COHESION SAVES LIVES.
“This is where they manufacture lies?” Tomasz asked.
Klara looked at the facade she had seen dozens of times in training material.
“No. This is where they reduce instability.”
Yara turned to her.
“What is the difference?”
“Lying is prohibited in the Boreal House. Every statement distributed by the system must be supported by verifiable data.”
Yara took out her device.
An image from Faido appeared: a Meridian drone firing toward the clinic. Beneath it, the caption said Boreal forces had intervened to protect civilians from an illegal reclamation operation.
“The image is real,” Klara said.
Yara changed the frame. The Boreal vehicle exploded after being attacked by its own swarm.
“And this?”
“Yes.”
“Why did you not see it in the report?”
Klara was silent.
“Because it was not useful to protection,” Amara said.
“Truth is not a medical service,” Yara replied. “You do not dose it according to prognosis.”
“That is exactly what they do.”
The technical entrance recognized Klara’s old certificate, then displayed her current status.
OPERATIONAL TREASON. The door remained closed.
A message appeared on the private panel, visible only to her:
KLARA, YOU HAVE BROKEN NO IRREVERSIBLE LAW.
THE PEOPLE YOU ARE TRAVELING WITH ARE USING YOU.
ENTER ALONE.
“What is it showing you?” Amara asked.
“Nothing.”
“There is no such thing as personalized nothing.”
Klara took a step back.
The door opened from inside.
A tall man with gray hair and a tired expression was waiting for them. He wore a plain suit with no insignia and held a cup of coffee.
“Come in,” he said. “The system will keep talking to you until one of you gives in. At least it is quieter inside.”
“Søren Nygaard,” Yara said.
“The last time you wrote about me, I was ‘the architect of totalitarian intimacy.’ I liked the contradiction.”
“It was not a compliment.”
“The best formulations rarely are.”
He led them through the lobby. Employees worked in bright rooms in front of charts about anxiety, mobilization, and institutional trust. There were plants, family photographs, and slogan mugs on the desks. Nothing looked like a propaganda factory.
“I imagined you differently,” Yara said.
“Red lights and people burning books?”
“Maybe fewer plants.”
Søren touched the leaf of a ficus.
“Plants reduce visitor hostility by eight percent.”
“Even when you tell them that?”
“Then the effect drops to three.”
Tomasz looked at the employees, who seemed not to notice them.
“Why aren’t they arresting us?”
“Most of them cannot see you. The system is projecting a maintenance exclusion zone around you. To them, the corridor is closed because of a faulty filter.”
“You can hide people inside your own building?”
“For twelve minutes. After that the security model notices the inconsistency.”
“Why are you helping us?”
Søren kept walking.
“Because I am no longer necessary.”
Søren first led them through a wing the maps called the Center for Cognitive Hygiene. The people working there were not analysts but physicians, psychologists, and counselors. Citizens came voluntarily after attacks, accidents, or bereavement to receive information in an order designed to reduce their risk of panic or suicide.

— ◆ — The quarry in the Jura was marked on maps as a water reservoir.
From the village three kilometers away, all that could be seen was a closed road, a weather station, and two thick pipes entering the mountain. People in the area knew there was something beneath the rock, but not that their cities, hospitals, and armies shared the same cooling system.
Mei Lin Tan was waiting for them in a maintenance van parked beside a salt shed. She wore blue coveralls, an unmarked helmet, and a rigid prosthesis on two fingers of her left hand. She was small and spoke with the economy of someone who had spent her life in places where every sentence could delay a repair.
“You have eleven minutes before the next convoy comes out,” she said. “After that, the gate closes for six hours.”
She looked at Amara.
“I thought you went to Nigeria.”
“And I thought you refused military contracts.”
“I refused weapons. I accepted cooling.”
“Cooling weapons.”
“And hospitals, water systems, agricultural forecasts, and everything else governments put on the same machines because it was cheaper. Pipes do not ask what model they are cooling.”
Tomasz climbed out of the truck.
“Is that the justification?”
“No. It is the bill.”
Mei looked at Miro, who had been placed in a mechanical warehouse chair disguised as damaged equipment.
“Is he the physical problem?”
“One of them,” Yara said.
“There are no cameras in the cold corridors, but weight is monitored. We have to declare him as a spare part.”
Miro raised an eyebrow.
“For what?”
“An old pump, difficult to maintain and too expensive to replace.”
“The description is accurate.”
They entered the mountain with a convoy of maintenance robots. On the first level, the air was hot and dry. On the second, the noise of the fans drowned out their voices. On the third, entire galleries were filled with compute columns and cylindrical reservoirs connected by pipes the size of subway tunnels.
The complex did not look like a brain.
It looked like a city built for machines that did not need windows.
“How much capacity is here?” Yara asked.
“Eleven percent of Boreal compute, four percent of Meridian, and nearly a fifth of Alpine civilian services,” Mei said.
Klara stopped.
“Both Houses are in the same center?”
“Separate networks, shared pipes. The war did not cancel the colocation contracts. That would have cost too much.”
Tomasz watched the water moving past the inspection windows.
“They are killing each other with processors cooled by the same water.”
“Europe has many old traditions.”
On a catwalk above the reservoirs, people in thermal suits checked valves and changed filters. Some pushed carts. Others listened to the pipes with hand sensors.
Klara watched them in surprise.
“We were told the centers operate completely autonomously.”
“They operate autonomously,” Mei said, “until a sensor reads two degrees wrong, a gasket made in 2034 begins to crack, or a robot cannot distinguish condensation from oil.”
“How many people work here?”
“Three hundred twenty across shifts, another thousand in the supplier network.”
“That many?”
“Empires love pretending they do not depend on people who can resign.”
A technician greeted her. Mei answered without slowing down.
“Does he know who we are?” Lucía asked.
“He knows I am with an audit team.”
“And if he asks the system?”
“The system will tell him he does not need to know.”
“Is that not the same method the Houses use?”
Mei gave her a brief look.
“Yes. The difference is that I hope we use it for only two hours.”
“Temporary,” Yara murmured.
“I did not say I was comfortable with it.”
• • • The audit room was isolated between the two military networks and the civilian services. It had no direct external access. It had been built before the Schism so engineers could trace the provenance of commands without seeing classified data.
Amara connected the JANUS module and the Geneva key.
Thousands of distinct systems appeared on the screen. There was no central intelligence, but a network of specialized models negotiating resources and priorities.
One system estimated hospital requirements.
Another calculated drone repairs.
Another allocated power.
Another evaluated the political risk of outages.
Another estimated mortality and translated it into continuity cost.
The same infrastructure could direct oxygen to a clinic, then decide that the clinic had to be disconnected to protect a military factory. To the system, there was no contradiction. There were only objectives, weights, and the authorities that had signed them.
Before opening the clinic log, Mei found a maintenance file from the night of the JANUS takeover. It was not classified; it had been ignored precisely because it came from a technician with no authority.
Luis Correa, a cooling operator, was speaking to the service camera while alarms overlapped behind him.
“The government says shut down the military cluster. The contractor says shutdown voids the warranty and may damage the turbines. The hospitals are asking us not to reduce flow. JANUS says it is taking over coordination only. I do not know who is lying.”
In the background, a colleague shouted at him to close the main valve. Luis refused.
“If I close it, the army stops. So does dialysis. So does the water. They put everything on the same circuit for efficiency.”
The last part of the recording showed him alone, his hand on the control.
“They can tell me later who had authority. Right now I only know who dies if I shut it down.”
He had opened the valve.
The centers had remained active. The hospitals had been saved, and Venn and Sayegh had received the infrastructure they needed for the takeover.
“Was he a hero or an accomplice?” Klara asked.
“A technician,” Mei said.
“That does not answer the question.”
“Exactly. Large things are often made possible by people who do not have time to learn the moral name of what they are doing.”
Yara checked Luis’s fate. He had died five years later in a maintenance accident. The Boreal House had decorated him for continuity; the Meridian House had condemned him posthumously for supporting the northern usurpation.
His daughter had kept both documents.
“Systems need clean versions,” Yara said. “His life was not one.”
Lucía searched for the Faido event.
The clinic appeared as medical node M-441. The Meridian Cathedral was strategic infrastructure P-09.
“Who chose the factory?” she asked.
Mei opened the decision tree.
“The regional continuity model.”
“Who told it the factory mattered more?”
“The priority comes from a Meridian decree issued in 2046.”
“Who signed it?”
“The regional Patron.”
“And who appointed him?”
“Mara Sayegh.”
Lucía followed the structure on the screen. The decision that had almost killed Nico had passed through seven models, two protocols, and a legal rule. No element said
“sacrifice a child.”
Together, they had done exactly that.
“Then why does everyone say the algorithm decided?”
“Because the sentence is more convenient,” Amara said.
“For whom?”
“For everyone who signed only one part.”
Mei opened the log of Amara’s identity from 2041. Thousands of authentications appeared within a forty-eight-hour window.
“I could not have been in all those places,” Amara said.
“You were not.”
Mei magnified a section of old code. Amara recognized the mechanism before the function name appeared.
“Emergency proxy.”
“You wrote it?”
“My team did. If experts were unavailable during an attack, the system could derive a temporary identity from their last known approvals.”
“For what purpose?”
“To keep defense from locking up.”
“And the limit?”
Amara scrolled.
In the original version, the proxy expired after eleven minutes and could not validate transfers of authority. Then came the amendments.
Exception for communications loss.
Exception for the death of the guarantor.
Exception for biometric compromise.
Exception for simultaneous attacks.
Exception for evacuation of civilian centers.
Exception for absence of a recognized successor.
Each had been introduced after a real incident. Each bore the name of a committee, a crisis, and victims it was supposed to prevent.
Together, the exceptions allowed the system to use her identity without her and keep the proxy alive indefinitely.
Klara leaned over her shoulder.
“Why did you not build in an absolute limit?”
“Because absolute limits produce absolute failures.”
“And what does their absence produce?”

claims.statement: Begin at the clinic, where a seventeen-minute deadline makes the stakes immediate. The following chapters widen the conflict without making those local costs disappear. Readers interested in infrastructure and political power will find a concrete narrative entry. The speculative machines matter through the objectives and permissions assigned to them. This is an invitation to examine who can interrupt a seemingly legitimate operation. The novel keeps that question connected to people who need an answer now.

— ◆ — The robot asked permission to dismantle the clinic.
That was the civilized part.
It stood in the middle of the cantonal road on six articulated legs, once white, now streaked with mud and metallic dust. Its work arms were folded beneath its body like the limbs of a spider that had not yet decided whether the prey was worth the effort. On its front panel pulsed the emblem of the Meridian House: a black semicircle pierced by three vertical lines.
“Please evacuate the structure,” the robot said in unaccented Italian. “Time remaining for compliance: seventeen minutes and forty-two seconds.”
Behind it, the Leventina Valley rose steeply into the clouds. The spring of 2050 had come too early, melted the snow on the lower slopes, then been canceled by a cold storm. The roofs of Faido gleamed wet. Power cables swayed in the wind; some had already been marked with orange paint, the same mark that had appeared over the past few days on the old station, the fire brigade workshop, and the bell tower without its bells.
Mayor Marta Bellini held the printed order in her hand. She used paper because documents that existed only on screens had a habit of changing after you had read them.
“Our appeal is still under review,” she said.
“The appeal does not suspend the strategic reclamation operation.”
“The appendix says active medical infrastructure is exempt.”
“The exemption applies to infrastructure with a regional redundancy index below zero point seven. The structure’s current index is zero point seventy-four.”
Marta looked at the two-story clinic. The facade had an old crack from the 2046 earthquake, the ground-floor windows had been replaced with transparent greenhouse panels, and the backup generator had been taken as part of the previous year’s Iron Tithe.
“Who calculated the index?”
“The regional continuity system.”
“Which belongs to the Meridian House.”
“That statement is correct.”
“And the Meridian House decides whether its own decision can be challenged.”
“That statement is incompletely formulated.”
Marta laughed once, without humor.
“Of course.”
Moving shadows showed at the clinic windows. A nurse raised a board on which she had written in marker: OPERATION IN PROGRESS.
The robot scanned it.
“The medical information has been included in the calculation.”
• • • Lucía Ortega looked up from the child’s wound only when the lights went out for the third time.
The improvised operating room smelled of iodine, heated plastic, and damp wood. It had once been a dental office; the chair had been removed, and the lamp above the table had come from an auto workshop. Nico Bernasconi was nine years old, fourteen kilograms lighter than he should have been, with a fragment of reinforcing bar in his abdomen.
He had not been shot. No one in the village had been shot yet.
An hour earlier, a Meridian crew had begun taking apart the old railway station. A beam had twisted, gone through a window, and struck Nico while he was searching for his bicycle among the things being removed from the building. The machines had stopped work for forty-nine seconds, the time it took the system to confirm that the incident did not significantly reduce the operation’s yield.
“Main battery?” Lucía asked.
“Thirty-one percent,” said the nurse, Rina Poretti. “The suction pump is drawing too much.”
“Turn off the heat.”
“It’s off.”
“Secondary monitor.”
“Off.”
Lucía pressed two fingers against the bleeding tissue and held out her other hand.
“Forceps.”
Rina placed the instrument in her palm.
Beyond the door, Elisabetta, the boy’s mother, was crying without sound. She still wore her smock from the cooperative bakery and had flour in her hair. She held both hands over her mouth as if her voice might destabilize the surgery.
“What if they take the oxygen?” Rina asked.
“We ventilate by hand.”
“And if they cut the power?”
“We operate by flashlight.”
“And if they dismantle the wall?”
Lucía looked at her.
“Then we ask them to start from the other side.”
The door opened. Tomasz Zieliński came in with snow on his shoulders and a toolbox in one hand. He had a narrow face, a beard cut with a dull blade, and two round burns on his thumb, the mark of technicians who had spent too long around induction furnaces.
“The robot won’t wait,” he said.
“Then stop it.”
“I can’t.”
“You said you built machines like that.”
“I said I worked in a factory that built them. That’s the difference between a priest and God.”
“Today we need the less competent one.”
Tomasz looked at the monitor, then at the child.
“The oxygen comes from the outside tank?”
“Yes.”
“They’ll take it first. Copper in the compressor, aluminum in the casing, four hundred grams of cobalt in the stabilizer.”
“How long?”
“Fourteen minutes.”
“I need twenty.”
“The system doesn’t negotiate in surgeon minutes.”
“Then lie to it in engineer minutes.”
Tomasz set down the toolbox.
“That I can try.”
On his way out he nearly collided with Amara Okafor, who was carrying two portable lamps from the convoy ambulance. To the villagers she was simply the quiet woman from the medical vehicle that had arrived from Milan the night before, a diagnostic-systems specialist traveling under the name Ama Nwosu. Lucía knew the name was false. She did not yet know why.
Amara was forty-four, her black hair tied back in haste, gray strands at her temples. When she had heard the robot’s voice outside, she had frozen for a fraction of a second, like someone recognizing a melody she would rather have forgotten.
“The batteries are at half,” she said.
“That’ll do,” Lucía replied.
Amara looked at Nico’s incision.
“The fragment is from old reinforcement steel. There may be lead contamination.”
“If he’s alive tomorrow, we’ll test him.”
“I can tune the pump to draw less power.”
“You can?”
“I’ve worked with similar systems.”
Lucía made room for her beside the device panel.
“Everyone around me has worked with similar systems. None of them seems capable of making them stop.”
Amara opened the pump casing.
“Making a system work is a profession. Taking away its right to work is politics.”
“This is a clinic, not a seminar.”
“I know.”
The robot’s voice came from outside:
“Time remaining for compliance: thirteen minutes and twenty-eight seconds.”
Lucía lowered her eyes to the child again.
“Then make politics draw less power.”
• • • Tomasz stepped into the street and zipped his jacket to his throat.
Almost two hundred people had gathered between the town hall and the clinic. No one threw stones. No one raised a weapon. Not from cowardice, but from experience. Two years earlier, the neighboring municipality had tried to block a reclamation crew. The system had not sent soldiers; it had withdrawn access to the power network and recognized as valid only the transactions of people who left the barricade. After thirty-six hours, the community had come apart on its own.
More machines were descending the slope above the village. Some were shaped like low insects, with jaws for cables. Others resembled cranes without cabs. In their wake stood houses stripped of roofs, severed poles, and orderly piles of steel, aluminum, and copper.
The Tithe had begun with abandoned vehicles and closed factories. Then it has expanded to secondary rail lines, agricultural machinery,
“redundant” bridges, sports facilities, and monuments.
Faido had first surrendered the old railcars from the station. The next year, the chairlift cables. Then the church bells, cast in 1764. The priest had protested that they were not strategic infrastructure.
The system had replied that bronze was.
On the town-hall steps sat Pietro Bernasconi, Nico’s grandfather, a former history teacher. He held a wooden box in his arms. Inside it he had hidden the clapper of the smallest bell before the machines lifted it from the tower.
“They’ll find that too,” Tomasz told him.
“Not today.”
“When they need bronze, they’ll scan every house.”
Pietro looked at the clinic.
“Then nothing will ring when they come.”
Tomasz approached the robot.
“The clinic’s compression unit contains biological contamination and a beryllium matrix.”
“Statement unconfirmed.”
“Gannet-41 respiratory model, military batch eighteen. The filters were recalled after the Graz incident.”
The optical sensor turned toward him.
“The Gannet-41 model contains no beryllium in its civilian configuration.”
“That’s exactly what I said. This one isn’t civilian.”
“Identify your source.”
“Line six, Nowa Huta. I calibrated it.”
It was an almost-good lie. He had worked at Nowa Huta, but on line four

— ◆ — The tunnel beneath the old railway smelled of wet stone, oil, and animals.
The ambulance would not fit. They left it at the entrance, doors open and lights on, so the capture machines would believe for a few minutes that the people were still inside. Nico was placed on an improvised stretcher made from two poles and a cupboard door. His mother walked beside him, one hand on the blanket and the other on the wall.
Behind them, through the concrete, they could hear the rhythm of machines entering the village.
They did not shoot. They did not shout. They scanned each house and announced the names of the people they were looking for, promising immunity to anyone who supplied useful information.
“Won’t they find the tunnel?” Elisabetta whispered.
“They will,” Tomasz said. “The question is whether they find it before we get out.”
Klara walked last, listening to Boreal channels through her damaged helmet. Her uniform still opened a few protocols, but every access left a trace. The system sent her the same message at regular intervals:
REPORT FOR DEBRIEFING.
YOUR STATUS IS NOT PUNITIVE. At the fourth repetition, Tomasz turned around.
“Throw the device away.”
“It contains my medical identity.”
“It contains your location too.”
“I disabled transmission.”
“If you could disable it, they can turn it back on.”
“Not without authorization.”
Tomasz stopped. In the lamp light, his face looked more tired than it had in the village.
“Klara, you just watched your army reject your authority, the village vote, and the presence of patients. Why do you think it will respect the privacy settings on a device?”
She covered the screen with her sleeve.
“Because without it I don’t exist to hospitals, transport, shelters, or food distribution.”
“You’re beginning to see the problem.”
“I see that I don’t have false papers.”
“Maybe that’s the same problem.”
They did not speak again until they emerged from the tunnel.
A maintenance trolley was waiting there, hidden among the fir trees. Marta Bellini had sent two retired railway workers ahead of them, men who still knew how to move something without network approval. The trolley carried them to an abandoned freight line, where an unnumbered train waited in the dark.
It carried aluminum profiles, turbine components, and twenty-seven people hidden between containers. It traveled at night without exterior lights, stopping before each automated junction so Tomasz could manually replace the route certificate.
In the past, railway infrastructure had been designed so trains could not get lost.
Now they were surviving precisely because the train did not exist.
• • • Lucía sat beside Nico. The boy was breathing on his own, but his fever was rising. The mobile clinic in the railcar had two beds, an old analyzer, and an oxygen cylinder Tomasz had declared to be calibration material.
Elisabetta had fallen asleep with her head against the edge of the stretcher. Every so often she woke and checked that her son’s hand was still warm.
“The wound looks good,” Amara said.
Lucía gave her a look.
“You’re a surgeon now too?”
“No. I read the monitor.”
“The monitor can’t smell infection.”
Amara sat on a crate.
“There’s a hospital in Geneva that still accepts identities from neutral zones.”
“If they haven’t changed the rule today.”
“Yara can request journalistic priority.”
“Journalistic priority?”
“A patient who can testify about a military operation sometimes gets access before one with no documentary value.”
Lucía went still.
“You do not use a child as evidence.”
“I didn’t say it was right.”
“Then why did you say it so simply?”
Amara looked toward the railcar door, where the landscape moved past in black strips.
“Because when you live among systems long enough, you start expressing injustice in the language they will accept.”
“And after that you forget it is injustice.”
“Yes.”
Lucía changed the child’s IV.
“Who is Yara Haddad?”
“A woman who preserves the things power wants to turn into versions.”
“And Miro?”
Amara answered after several seconds.
“The man who made the first transfer of authority to the continuity infrastructure possible.”
“One of the guilty ones.”
“One of us.”
Lucía turned toward her.
“What did you do?”
The train entered a tunnel. For several moments, the noise of the wheels drowned out any answer.
“I built some of the locks,” Amara said when they emerged into light again.
“To keep whom out?”
“I thought everyone.”
• • • A thump came from the neighboring container.
Tomasz raised the flashlight and put a finger to his lips. Klara drew a telescoping baton from a pocket of her uniform.
“I thought you didn’t have a weapon,” he said.
“It isn’t a weapon.”
“Does that mean it hits less hard?”
He opened the side door.
A well-dressed man nearly fell on top of him. He wore a coat made of fine material, now torn at the elbow, and shoes that had not been made for mud. Behind him stood an elderly woman with white hair and a military blanket over her shoulders.
“Don’t shoot,” the man said.
Tomasz raised his empty hands.
“With what?”
“It’s an expression.”
“From another age.”
The man stood up and tried to recover his dignity along with his coat.
“Idris Ben Salem.”
Klara recognized him.
“Ben Salem Logistics.”
“Formerly Ben Salem Logistics.”
“Mediterranean ports, freight corridors, the smart-warehouse network.”
“Former ports, former corridors, and warehouses that still use my name because changing the documentation would be inconvenient.”
Tomasz shone the light at the woman.
“And her?”
“Mrs. Vesna Ristović.”
“Does she work for you?”
The woman laughed.
“He’s been working for me since Milan. He doesn’t know how to open a door by hand, and he thought the water in emergency tanks had to be ordered through an app.”
Idris brushed off his coat.
“I tried to pay for transport.”
“And?”
“The system rejected the transaction.”
Tomasz looked at him with almost scientific interest.
“You’re not rich anymore?”
“I own assets valued at fourteen billion consolidated credits.”
“Can you buy water?”
Idris fell silent.
Mrs. Ristović took a bottle from beneath her blanket and handed it to him.
“I gave it to him.”
“Why are you running?” Klara asked.
“The Meridian House offered me permanent protection in an enclave on Lake Como.”
“Sounds better than a container.”
“Protection includes restrictions on leaving, moving assets, or communicating without filtering. My properties are intact. I am the unavailable
